title: A Federal Judge Just Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. The White House Says It Will Appeal.
excerpt: Judge Leo Sorokin ruled the fee was an unauthorized tax — the same constitutional logic the Supreme Court used to strike down Trump's tariffs in February.
body:
For nine months, a single presidential proclamation did what years of congressional gridlock could not: it effectively froze H-1B hiring in the United States.

In September 2025, President Donald Trump announced a $100,000 fee on every new H-1B visa application — a fifty-fold increase over the $2,000 to $5,000 that employers had previously paid. The stated rationale was that the program had been "abused for decades." The practical effect was immediate and dramatic: by February, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had received just 85 payments at the new rate. The pipeline that delivers hundreds of thousands of skilled workers — overwhelmingly Indian — to American employers each year had all but seized up.

On June 8, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston struck the fee down in its entirety.

## The Ruling

Sorokin's 42-page opinion turned on a single question: was the $100,000 payment a fee or a tax? The Trump administration argued it was a lawful monetary penalty the president could impose under the Immigration and Nationality Act, which gives him broad authority to restrict entry of foreign nationals he deems "detrimental to the interests of the United States."

The judge disagreed. "The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," he wrote. And only Congress can levy a tax.

Sorokin drew a direct line to the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in February that struck down Trump's sweeping tariffs imposed under emergency powers. Under the logic of that decision, the president similarly lacked authority under immigration law to impose what amounts to a revenue-generating measure. The ruling vacated the fee "in its entirety."

The lawsuit was brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general who argued the fee amounted to an unauthorized tax on employers seeking to fill specialized roles in technology, engineering, and medicine.

## The Industry Response

The H-1B program issues 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 reserved for holders of advanced degrees, typically approved for three- to six-year terms. Big Tech companies — Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and increasingly AI firms like Anthropic and OpenAI — are the program's largest beneficiaries.

The fee's chilling effect was not subtle. Court filings documented a dramatic collapse in applications. Companies that had relied on the H-1B pipeline for years found themselves unable to justify the cost, and many shifted hiring to overseas offices in India, Canada, and the U.K. instead.

For Indian professionals — who account for roughly 75 per cent of all H-1B approvals in a typical year — the ruling removes a barrier that had made American employment prohibitively expensive for all but the most senior and specialized roles.

## What Happens Next

The White House has signalled it will appeal. Spokesperson Taylor Rogers said the administration is "confident this order will be reversed," noting that a separate federal judge in Washington, D.C., had upheld a "nearly identical order" in a case brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

That split between courts — one judge saying Trump can impose the fee, another saying he cannot — makes it likely the issue will eventually reach a federal appeals court. Legal observers say the Supreme Court's tariff ruling may have set a precedent that weakens the administration's position, but the outcome is far from certain.

The $100,000 fee had prompted at least three separate lawsuits. The Trump administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

The H-1B program remains the primary legal pathway through which Indian tech workers enter the American workforce. The $100,000 fee, even during its brief lifespan, accelerated a shift already under way: companies rerouting talent to offices in Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Toronto rather than bringing workers to the U.S.

If the ruling survives appeal, the immediate effect will be a restoration of pre-September hiring economics. But the broader trend — of an American immigration system that has become increasingly hostile to skilled migration — is not something a single court ruling can reverse. The EB-2 green card cap for Indians was hit earlier this month, freezing the queue until October. The EB-5 investor visa category has also been exhausted for Indian applicants.

For hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals waiting in backlogs that stretch decades, the court's decision is a reprieve, not a resolution.
